query: For a titanium- and nickel-containing high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state, whose elevated-temperature mechanical performance remains unestablished when titanium and nickel serve as primary constituents rather than additions, what single testable intervention hypothesis could produce better mechanical properties under elevated-temperature or extreme-environment testing than the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, mechanism, predicted relative outcome, applicable composition and test-regime boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled minor Mo addition (on the order of 1–2 at%) to a titanium–nickel high-entropy alloy followed by a tailored homogenization/aging treatment induces formation of stable Mo-rich nano-precipitates that hinder dislocation motion, thereby enhancing elevated-temperature mechanical properties compared to the alloy without such an intervention.
generation.material_initial_state: A Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy in a single-phase solid-solution state where Ti and Ni are the primary constituents.
generation.intervention: Introduce a minor (∼1–2 at%) Mo addition into the alloy composition and apply a homogenization heat treatment followed by an aging process to promote the formation of nano-scale, Mo-rich precipitates.
generation.conditions: The intervention should be evaluated under elevated-temperature mechanical test regimes (e.g., tensile and creep tests at temperatures around 600–700°C) where the precipitates remain stable. The alloy composition must remain within the single-phase solid-solution region aside from the intentionally induced precipitates.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of stable, uniformly dispersed Mo-rich nano-precipitates within the Ti–Ni solid-solution matrix.
generation.mechanism: The added Mo partitions to form nano-precipitates during homogenization and aging. These precipitates act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain boundary sliding, providing enhanced precipitation strengthening and improving high-temperature yield and creep resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Mo-added and heat-treated alloy will exhibit improved elevated-temperature mechanical performance—namely, increased yield strength, enhanced creep resistance, and higher hardness—compared to the baseline alloy without Mo and without the specialized thermal treatment.
generation.baseline: The Ti–Ni high-entropy alloy without Mo addition and without the homogenization/aging treatment.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects are expected to manifest under testing conditions up to approximately 700°C, within the compositional limits that maintain single-phase stability aside from nano-precipitate formation. Beyond this temperature regime or with deviations in Mo content, the predicted mechanical improvement may diminish or alter.
generation.uncertainty: While similar precipitation strengthening mechanisms have been observed in related Ni-containing systems, the exact optimal Mo concentration, precipitate size, volume fraction, and heat treatment parameters for the Ti–Ni matrix remain to be established. The degree of improvement may also be sensitive to the processing route and impurity levels.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloy samples: one set with a 1–2 at% Mo addition subjected to the prescribed homogenization and aging treatment, and a control set without Mo and without the additional heat treatments. Conduct elevated-temperature tensile and creep tests (e.g., at 600–700°C) while characterizing the microstructure (using TEM or similar techniques) to verify the formation of Mo-rich nano-precipitates.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength at elevated temperatures
Creep rate under sustained load at test temperature
Nanoindentation hardness measurements at high temperature
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis to identify and quantify nano-precipitates
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-added, heat-treated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in yield strength, creep resistance, or hardness compared to the control samples, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal the formation of a stable population of Mo-rich precipitates, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory elements, including Rhenium (Re), Molybdenum (Mo), Niobium (Nb), Tantalum (Ta), and Tungsten (W) [] are very important for improving mechanical properties in advanced alloys such as Titanium alloys and Nickel-base superalloys. Generally, elements with a melting point higher than Titanium (Ti), such as Chromium (Cr), Hafnium (Hf), Osmium (Os), Ruthenium (Ru), Vanadium (V), and Zirconium (Zr) are also classified as refractory elements. In Titanium alloys, refractory elements, especially Mo and W, are all beta stabilizers and possess a strong solid solution strengthening characteristic []. Nb forms Ni3Nb γ phase in Nickel-base superalloys such as Inconel 718 []. The improved creep resistance of the sixth generation superalloy TMS-238 mainly results from Re and Ru additions []. Refractory alloys also play significant roles in industry. In the second generation nuclear power plants, the most-used materials for fuel cladding are Zircoloy 2 and Zircoloy 4. The Niobium alloy C103 is used for the nozzle extension of satellites []. AbstractCo-free body-centered cubic (bcc) high-entropy alloys (HEAs) are prepared, and the elevated mechanical property and corrosion property of the Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mox (x = 0 and 0.1) alloys are studied. The Vickers hardness (HV) of the as-homogenized state is between HV 350 and HV 400. Both alloys are provided with nano-scale NiAl-rich B2 precipitates which contribute to the strength at high-temperature. In addition, adding Mo in the present alloy strengthens by σ phase. Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5Mo0.1 exhibited outstanding tensile properties, with a yield strength of 413 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 430 MPa in the elevated tensile test at 600 °C, which is better than that of Al0.4CrFe1.5MnNi0.5 alloy. Through potentiodynamic polarization testing in 0.5 M H2SO4 solution and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), it is shown that adding Mo can effectively reduce the corrosion current density and improve the impedance of passive film, since the passivation layer is formed and stable.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, body centered cubic, NiAl precipitates, high-temperature tensile, corrosion, EIS

reading.lever: Add a controlled minor Mo addition to the Ti-Ni HEA, then use a homogenization/aging treatment to induce stable nano-precipitates.
reading.why: This approach, demonstrated in related Ni-containing systems to enhance high-temperature strength, directly targets phase stability and strengthening in the Ti-Ni HEA.
